query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled minor amount of Sn to a single-phase fcc FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy will trigger the formation of a BCC phase (and associated nano-precipitates) that increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain wall pinning, thus boosting the coercive field above the ~100 Oe level found in pure fcc FeCoNi alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi (or a closely matched derivative) exhibiting high saturation magnetization and low coercivity (below 100 Oe).
generation.intervention: Introduce a small, controlled addition of Sn into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed under conditions that favor a mixed-phase microstructure (i.e., promoting a partial transformation from FCC to BCC) with well-dispersed nano-precipitates at room temperature; composition boundaries similar to those in FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx systems (e.g., up to 10 atomic % Sn) may be used.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a BCC phase and associated nano-precipitates within the primarily fcc matrix, creating additional phase boundaries that serve as domain wall pinning sites.
generation.mechanism: Sn addition alters the phase stability, driving part of the material from low-anisotropy FCC structure to a higher-anisotropy BCC structure and precipitate formation. Increased magnetocrystalline anisotropy and stronger domain wall pinning from the BCC phase and the nano-interfaces collectively elevate the coercive field.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coercive field is expected to exceed 100 Oe, while high saturation magnetization is largely maintained relative to a single-phase fcc FeCoNi baseline.
generation.baseline: Properties of single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its closely related compositions that exhibit coercivity values below 100 Oe.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable under room-temperature magnetic measurements, for alloys with limited Sn additions (e.g., up to about 10 atomic %), and when processed to allow phase separation without severely compromising overall magnetic performance.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Sn concentration required to achieve the optimal balance of FCC/BCC phases, the quantification of the coercivity increase, and potential trade-offs with saturation magnetization require further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of FeCoNi-based alloys with incrementally increasing Sn content (e.g., 0, 2, 5, and 10 atomic %). Use controlled processing (casting, heat treatment, and cooling) to promote phase evolution. Characterize the phase fractions using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and measure the magnetic properties, especially coercivity, using a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) at room temperature.
measurements: XRD for phase identification and determination of FCC/BCC phase fractions
TEM for microstructural analysis (e.g., nano-precipitate distribution)
VSM for coercive field and saturation magnetization measurements
DSC to monitor any phase transition behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-doped alloys do not exhibit a significant increase in the coercive field (i.e., if coercivity remains at or below ~100 Oe) and if no appreciable formation of a BCC phase or associated pinning microstructure is detected relative to the pure FCC sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work exhibits the effects of Sn addition on the magnetic properties and microstructure of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The results show all the samples consist of a mixed structure of face-centered-cubic (FCC) phase and body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nano-precipitates in BCC matrix. It also shows that the Curie temperatures (Tc) of the FCC phase and the saturation magnetization (Ms) of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs increase greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases after the addition of Sn into FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA. The thermomagnetic curves indicate that the phases of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs will transform from FCC with low Tc to BCC phase with high Tc at temperature of 600–700 K. This work provides a new idea for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs for their potential application as soft magnets to be used at high temperatures.

However, there is only little change for the value of magnetization as the temperature continues to increase. This is because only a small number of FCC phase transform to BCC phase according to the results of XRD in Figure 1 and DSC curves in Figure S1. Therefore, it can be concluded that the addition of a minor amount of Sn can obviously increase the Curie temperature of FCC phase. The phases of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs will transform from FCC with low Tc to BCC phase with high Tc at temperature of 600–700 K, which leads to the increase of magnetization. This provides a new idea for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs for their potential application as soft magnets to be used at high temperature.
